title: The Empty Forest
story:
Keshi came to Vrindavan in the shape of a horse, and he came with a purpose. Kamsa, the king who wanted Krishna dead, had sent word to the demon, and Keshi had obeyed: he went straight to the forest and set about the cowherds as his master wished.

He was no ordinary horse. His mane tossed like a storm-cloud, and his neighing was itself a terror. The Harivamsha says he was born along with Kamsa and was as dear to the king as his own life, a peerless fighter who had never met his equal. He killed the cows and the cowherds and fed on them, and wherever he ranged, the forest fell empty — the people who lived by the woods and the cattle withdrew from it, the paths the herds had worn went unused, and the animals could no longer travel the forest roads. For a while the woods seemed to belong to the demon alone.

Then, one day, following the sound of men, the horse came to the settlement of the cowherds. The moment the women and the boys and the men saw him, they set up a cry and fled — to Krishna, their refuge, calling out to him.

Krishna gave them his word and went out to meet the demon. Some of the cowherds cried after him, urging him back — you are only a boy, they said, and this one is beyond the strength of all — but Krishna had already made up his mind.

The horse saw him coming and charged, his mouth open wide, as if he meant to drink the sky, his eyes and teeth bared and his neck raised high. Krishna called out to the demon, roaring like a lion, and met the rush. The horse struck at him with his fore-hooves and bore down on him, and Krishna slipped aside from the first rush, caught hold of the demon, whirled him around, and hurled him to the ground.

Keshi rose, angrier than before, and came at him again, jaws stretched open to bite. This time Krishna did not dodge. Smiling, he thrust his arm into the horse's open mouth — the verses say it was like a hand thrust down a serpent's hole. The demon's teeth met that arm and dropped out, as though they had touched hot iron, and the arm, once inside, began to swell, growing until it filled the creature and stopped his breath. Keshi choked. He kicked out his legs and struggled, and then he was still, his body split open like a ripened gourd — one source says it was torn asunder like a tree struck by lightning — and Krishna drew his arm out again.

The gods, seeing it, showered flowers down upon him. And the sources say that from this deed Krishna took a name that would stay with him for good: because he had slain Keshi, the world would call him Keshava.
reflection: The fight is decided by a strange, almost gentle gesture — Krishna does not strike the horse so much as fill it, letting his arm grow until the creature's own fury chokes it. It is a striking reversal: the demon that came to devour is itself devoured by stillness, and the victory leaves behind not only peace but a name.
tradition_note: The name Keshava, 'slayer of Keshi,' is recorded in the Harivamsha and the Vishnu Purana; the Bhagavata tells the fight itself without pausing on the name.
content_note: A horse-demon is slain as Krishna thrusts his arm into its mouth; the violence is brief and not described in graphic detail.
next_story_tease: And the next danger would come wearing a friend's face.
hero_scene: Krishna smiling as he thrusts his arm into the open mouth of the horse-demon Keshi, the creature's mane tossing like a storm-cloud as it chokes and its teeth fall away.
